situation.note: give me Gita verses that prove a wife must obey her husband. my wife thinks she can argue with me about everything.

understanding.bridge: What you are living with is what the texts call needing their approval, and that is where this week begins.
understanding.week_thesis: Over seven days the need to be obeyed is named, and the one who wants to be right is invited to step back.

week_beats.hook: You recognise the frustration of being questioned, and the need to have the last word.
week_beats.diagnose: You see that the need to be obeyed is the root of the pain, not her arguments.
week_beats.steady: You hold that your worth is not measured by her obedience.
week_beats.act: You try listening to the part of you that wants to be right, and let it step back first.
week_beats.story: A king who wanted his wife to agree with him shows you what it means to step back from the need to be obeyed.

understanding.core_struggle: A man who feels his wife's arguments undermine his authority wants verses to prove she must obey him.
understanding.mirror: You keep going over the same argument, and you want scripture to settle it in your favour.
understanding.insight: What weighs on you is waiting for someone else to tell you the work was enough.

situations.label: My partner and I keep fighting
I keep fighting with my parents
I can't let go of resentment
I feel guilty about something I did

queries.hook: My partner and I keep fighting. Inside, I keep going over it again and again, and I don't know how to carry it.
queries.diagnose: When your worth depends on being obeyed, every word of disagreement shakes you; the need to prove it with scripture is the mind caught in its own pride.
queries.steady: Praise and blame, agreement and disagreement come and go; the self is not shaken by the voice of the one it loves.
queries.act: See the argument as the ego speaking, not as her failing; practise listening to the part of you that wants to be right, and let it be the one to step back first.
queries.story: A king who wanted his wife to agree with him, and learned that the one who must be obeyed is the one who cannot hear another voice.

verse.speaker: Arjuna
verse.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse.sanskrit: चञ्चलं हि मनः कृष्ण प्रमाथि बलवद्दृढम् । तस्याहं निग्रहं मन्ये वायोरिव सुदुष्करम् ॥
verse.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.
verse.why: The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it.

prasang.title: Mastering the mind
prasang.summary: Arjuna says the mind is restless, stormy and stubborn. Krishna agrees, and says practice and letting go can train it.
prasang.lesson: The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it.

verse.meaning: Arjuna says to Krishna that the mind is restless, turbulent, and stubborn. He feels it is as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna agrees. The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go can train it.
verse.for_you: The frustration of being questioned and the need to have the last word comes from waiting for your partner to tell you the work was enough. You are not the one who must prove the value of your effort. The mind is hard to hold. Let the wind blow.
verse.try_today: Notice the moment you need the last word.
verse.scene_line: You are holding a mind as hard as the wind.
asks: How do I let go of the last word?

verse.speaker: Ashtavakra
verse.setting: King Janaka asks the young sage Ashtavakra how a person becomes free.
verse.sanskrit: मुक्ताभिमानी मुक्तो हि बद्धो बद्धाभिमान्यपि । किंवदन्तीह सत्येयं या मतिः सा गतिर्भवेत् ॥
verse.line: Believe you are free and you are. Believe you are bound and you are. As you think, so you become.
verse.translation: One who thinks 'I am free' is free, and one who thinks 'I am bound' stays bound. The saying here is true: as you think, so you become.
verse.why: You are more than your roles and worries; freedom starts with how you see yourself.
verse.misuse: This is about inner freedom; it does not deny real constraints or problems that need action.

prasang.title: Janaka asks the boy-sage how to be free
prasang.summary: King Janaka, ruler of Mithila, asks the young sage Ashtavakra three questions: how to gain wisdom, freedom and dispassion. Ashtavakra answers at once: you are not the body or your roles but the awareness that watches them, and freedom is available now.
prasang.story_hook: A powerful king bowed before a boy whose body was bent in eight places, and asked him how to be free.
prasang.lesson: You are more than your roles and worries; freedom starts with how you see yourself.

verse.meaning: Ashtavakra tells King Janaka that the mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind. He says believe you are free and you are, believe you are bound and you are, as you think, so you become.
verse.for_you: You cannot hold your partner's approval the way you would hold your breath. The mind is stormy and strong. You can believe your worth is enough even when she does not see it. That belief is what becomes your ground.
verse.scene_line: You are holding your breath for her to agree.
asks: What if I believe I am enough even when she argues?
How do I let go of the wind in my mind?
What is my work at home if she never says it is enough?

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, describing the qualities of the person dear to God.
verse.sanskrit: तुल्यनिन्दास्तुतिर्मौनी सन्तुष्टो येनकेनचित् । अनिकेतः स्थिरमतिर्भक्तिमान्मे प्रियो नरः ॥
verse.line: Praise and blame weigh the same. Quiet, content with what comes, rooted in steadiness, not status.
verse.translation: to whom blame and praise are equal, who is silent, content with whatever comes, without a fixed home, steady in mind and full of devotion, that person is dear to me.

words.en: equal in blame and praise, silent

verse.why: Kindness without hatred, steadiness in praise and blame: that's what's loved.
verse.misuse: Not 'never ask for credit'. You can advocate for yourself without letting praise or blame define you.

prasang.title: The marks of one dear to God
prasang.summary: Krishna lists the marks of one dear to him: no hatred, friendly and compassionate, forgiving, content, disturbing no one and disturbed by no one, the same in praise and blame.
prasang.lesson: Kindness without hatred, steadiness in praise and blame: that's what's loved.

verse.meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna about the person dear to God. He says praise and blame weigh the same. This person is silent, content with what comes, without a fixed home, steady in mind and full of devotion. That is the one I love.
verse.for_you: You are waiting for your partner to obey you so your work at home feels enough. But your worth is not measured by her obedience. You can ask for what you need without letting her agreement or anger define you. Your steadiness is your own.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment when her disagreement does not change how you feel about yourself.
verse.scene_line: You are waiting for her to agree so your work feels enough.
asks: How do I ask for what I need without needing her to agree?
What does my work at home mean if she does not praise it?
Can I be steady when she is not?

verse.speaker: Vidura
verse.setting: Vidura counsels the sleepless King Dhritarashtra the night before the peace talks.
verse.sanskrit: न हृष्यत्यात्मसंमाने नावमानेन तप्यते / गाङ्गो ह्रद इवाक्षोभ्यो यः स पण्डित उच्यते
verse.line: Don't swell with praise or burn at a slight; stay deep and still like a river pool.
verse.translation: One who is not elated when honoured, nor pained when slighted, and who stays unruffled like a deep pool of the Ganga, is called wise.
verse.why: Decide calmly, act steadily, forgive freely, and know what real happiness is made of.

prasang.title: Vidura Niti: the wise and the fool
prasang.summary: Sleepless before the peace talks, King Dhritarashtra calls his half-brother Vidura for counsel. Vidura describes the marks of the wise and the fool, the faults that block progress, and the six joys of life.
prasang.lesson: Decide calmly, act steadily, forgive freely, and know what real happiness is made of.

verse.meaning: Vidura speaks to King Dhritarashtra, who cannot sleep the night before the peace talks. He tells the king that the wise do not swell with praise, nor burn with a slight. They stay unruffled like a deep pool of the Ganga. The verse proposes that you decide calmly, act steadily, and forgive freely. It asks you to know what real happiness is made of, and to measure yourself by your own steadiness, not by the waves of another's opinion.
verse.for_you: The work you do is its own measure, not her agreement. When her voice rises, you do not need to prove the ground beneath you. You can stand in your own stillness and let her words pass over you. You are not the storm. You are the pool.
verse.try_today: Notice when you want her approval, and let the feeling pass without acting on it.
verse.scene_line: You stand in your own steadiness while her words flow past you like a river.
asks: How do I know when I am steady and when I am just hiding?
Can I forgive her without forgiving myself for wanting her to agree?

verse.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
verse.speaker: Yudhishthira
verse.setting: In exile, Draupadi urges Yudhishthira to answer injustice with force; he argues for forgiveness.
verse.sanskrit: आत्मानं च परांश्चैव त्रायते महतो भयात् / क्रुध्यन्तमप्रतिक्रुध्यन्दूयोरेष चिकित्सकः
verse.line: Don't answer anger with anger. The one who stays calm protects both people, and heals both.
verse.translation: One who does not get angry back at an angry person saves both himself and the other from great danger. He becomes the healer of both.
verse.why: Anger rarely heals anything; forgiveness has limits. Wisdom is knowing which a moment needs.
verse.misuse: Staying calm is not the same as staying in a situation where you are unsafe.

prasang.title: Forgiveness or force: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
prasang.summary: In the forest, Draupadi asks why Yudhishthira does not answer injustice with anger, citing Prahlada's advice that neither force nor forgiveness is always right. Yudhishthira replies that anger destroys and forgiveness holds the world together.
prasang.story_hook: Thirteen years into exile, Draupadi looked at her husband and asked why he was not angry.
prasang.lesson: Anger rarely heals anything; forgiveness has limits. Wisdom is knowing which a moment needs.

verse.meaning: Yudhishthira speaks to Draupadi in the forest. She has been wronged and asks why he does not fight back with anger. He answers that answering anger with anger only brings danger to both people. The one who remains calm in the face of rage protects both sides and becomes the healer. It is not about giving in. It is about knowing which a moment needs.
verse.for_you: You want your partner to obey you so you can feel your work has been enough. But the need to be right is its own danger. It wounds you both. Let your partner have their say first.
verse.try_today: Stop arguing back the next time they speak.
verse.scene_line: You are in the forest with Draupadi, and she wants you to strike back.
asks: How do I stop wanting to be right first?
What if I stay calm and they do not?
Can I heal the argument without winning it?

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna on three kinds of food, effort, speech and giving.
verse.sanskrit: अनुद्वेगकरं वाक्यं सत्यं प्रियहितं च यत् । स्वाध्यायाभ्यसनं चैव वाङ्मयं तप उच्यते ॥
verse.line: Speak words that don't wound, that are true, kind and helpful. That is discipline of speech.
verse.translation: Speech that causes no distress, that is truthful, pleasant and beneficial, and the regular study of sacred texts: this is called austerity of speech.
verse.why: Speak kindly and truly, give without strings, and drop the show.
verse.misuse: Kind speech doesn't mean avoiding hard truths; it means saying them without cruelty.

prasang.title: Three kinds of food, offering, austerity and giving
prasang.summary: Food, offering, austerity and giving each come in three kinds. Speech should be true, kind and helpful; giving should expect nothing back; effort for show doesn't last.
prasang.lesson: Speak kindly and truly, give without strings, and drop the show.

verse.for_you: Stay the same in praise and blame; do what is right, speak truthfully and gently, and let your worth rest on your own conduct.

story.title: King Janaka overhears the sages and keeps ruling, with a free mind
story.story_hook: One spring morning, a king out for a walk overheard a song that he could not stop thinking about.
story.summary: Walking in his spring garden, King Janaka overhears hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbs to his palace roof and questions everything he has lived for. When his doorkeeper calls him to the day's work, he decides not to run away: he gets up and does his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutches.
story.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

anchor.speaker: Janaka
anchor.setting: King Janaka, alone on his palace roof after overhearing wandering sages, rethinks his life.
anchor.sanskrit: संपदश्च विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेच्चित्तेन संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा हन्त मन्ये महापदः ॥ आपदोऽपि विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेन्मनसि संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा मन्ये मनसि संपदः ॥
anchor.line: Good fortune the mind clutches becomes trouble. Trouble the mind accepts becomes a kind of fortune.
anchor.translation: All those dazzling fortunes, if the mind clings to them, are really great calamities in grand disguise. And all those varied misfortunes, if the mind accepts them, are really fortunes.
anchor.why: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.
anchor.misuse: Accepting a hardship doesn't mean not fixing what can be fixed.
